text: A distribution describes which values a variable takes and how often it takes them. Center and spread are two numbers that summarize it; shape is the rest of the story. Two variables can share the same mean and standard deviation and still look completely different. This lesson gives you the vocabulary for shape — symmetry, skew, tails, and peaks.

When you look at a histogram, ask four questions. Symmetry: is the left side a mirror of the right? Skew: does one side have a long tail — right-skewed, like incomes, means most values are small and a few are huge; left-skewed means a long tail toward low values. Peaks: one, called unimodal, two, called bimodal, or more? And tails: are extreme values rare or surprisingly common?

The mean is pulled by extreme values while the median is not, giving a handy rule: in a right-skewed distribution the mean tends to be larger than the median, and in a left-skewed one, smaller. Generating three illustrative datasets — symmetric, right-skewed, left-skewed — and measuring each confirms it.

The symmetric data has mean 49.8, median 49.7, and skewness near 0. The right-skewed data has a mean of 30.3 well above its median of 21.3, with skewness 1.97. The left-skewed data flips both, mean 90.0 below median 93.0, skewness negative 1.9. Skewness is a single number for direction and strength — positive means a long right tail, negative a long left tail, and values beyond about 1 are usually considered strongly skewed.

Kurtosis describes how heavy the tails are compared with a normal bell curve. pandas's kurt returns excess kurtosis, where 0 corresponds to normal. Our symmetric data gave about negative 0.03, essentially normal, while the skewed data gave 5.87 and 4.98 — much heavier tails. Kurtosis is noisy on small samples, so treat it as a rough hint and let a chart decide.

Some distributions have two peaks because two different groups are mixed together — say, a local courier and a long-distance courier. Concatenating two normal distributions centered at 20 and 60 gives a mean and median that both say 40, a perfectly symmetric-looking summary. Yet a histogram shows almost nobody near 40 — in our run, only 7 of 5,000 values fell between 32 and 48.

Summary statistics can hide the truth here, and a bimodal shape is usually a sign you should ask whether you're really looking at two subgroups. For strong skew: report the median and IQR instead of, or alongside, the mean; transform the data — a logarithm compresses a long right tail, turning a skewness of 1.97 into about negative 0.47; and choose methods that fit, since many classical tests assume roughly symmetric data.

To recap: shape completes the picture beyond center and spread — check symmetry, skew, peaks, and tails. Compare mean and median for a quick skew check, use skew and kurt for numbers, and be suspicious when a mean sits where there's no actual data.
